background.definition: Dysthymia is a clinical syndrome characterized by 3 to 4 major depressive episode symptoms with a core symptom of depressed mood for at least 2 years in adults and 1 year in children and adolescents, and no more than 2 months without symptoms, that causes severe distress or occupational, social or other functional impairment. Dysthymia is now classified under persistent depressive disorder (PDD), combined with chronic major depressive disorder (MDD).

list.listitem: General population: 25/1000 persons/year.
Primary care patient populations: 51/1000 persons/year.
Global pooled prevalence based on data from 30 countries was 1.55% (95% CI 1.50-1.60).

Using the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual-5 (DSM-5), lifetime estimates of PDD based on interviews with a random sample of 3729 individuals living in an urban area were 15.2% for PDD with persistent major depressive episode and 3.3% for PDD with pure dysthymia.

Among children and young people with intellectual disorders, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 databases and 21 studies found estimated pooled prevalence for dysthymic disorders of 2.1% among children and 6.9% among adolescents.
More common among: women, people less than 65 years old, young people with low income.

Authors of a systematic review of 28 studies concluded that patients with chronic depression had an earlier onset of depressive symptoms, higher rates of psychiatric comorbidities, and a more complicated treatment course than patients suffering from non-chronic MDD.

Patients with dysthymia compared with non-affected patients are more likely to use health services, 3 times more likely to use mental health services in a general medical setting, and 5 times more likely to use mental health specialty services.
Individuals with dysthymia who are current smokers are less likely to quit or remain abstinent from smoking than those without the disorder.

Both dysthymia and major depression increased the risk of dementia nearly two-fold and increased mortality rates among older veterans. The adjusted hazard ratio for mortality among those with dysthymia was 1.4 (95% CI 1.3-1.5).

Patients with depressive disorders have high rates of sexual dysfunction; in one meta-analysis including patients with PDD, overall sexual dysfunction was found in 82.8% of women (95% CI: 74.7-90.8) and 63.3% of men (95% CI: 52.8-73.7).
Individuals with dysthymic disorder are at higher risk of developing obesity within 3 years compared to those with nonatypical MDD or no history of depressive disorder (OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.3-2.1).
Specific etiology unknown.
Some patients may have a genetic predisposition to environmental (prolonged exposure to stressful events), psychological (poor coping skills), or physiologic (sleep disorders) cofactors.
Exact pathophysiologic pathways are unknown; disease expression is likely due to heterogeneous mechanisms.
PDD may involve deficiencies of neurotransmitters (eg, norepinephrine, serotonin, dopamine) or other hormones (cortisol); alternatively, receptors for these substances may be dysfunctional.

Immune system dysregulation may play a role. In one study, the serum of 12 patients with dysthymic disorder exhibited aberrant cytokine and chemokine expression compared with 12 patients with MDD and 20 age-, sex-, and body mass index-matched healthy controls which appeared to resolve following treatment with anti-depressants.

Authors of a meta-analysis of neuroimaging experiments found inconsistent results and no significant differences in cognitive or emotional processing between adult patients with unipolar depression and healthy control subjects. Investigators in one study found differences in white matter microstructure between 25 boys with PDD and 25 typically-developing children.
No specific recommendations exist regarding screening for persistent depressive disorder. Consider depression screening if adequate follow-up can be assured for patients who screen positive.
The most prominent characteristic is at least 2 years of persistently depressed mood in adults or 1 year in children and adolescents. C
Most patients also experience chronic fatigue, low energy, guilt or a sense of worthlessness, and difficulty concentrating or making decisions. B
Mild but chronic symptoms lead to significant distress or cumulative functional impairment. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Requires 5 or more major depressive episode symptoms and minimum symptom duration of 2 weeks or more; the core symptom may be either depressed mood or anhedonia
Requires 2 to 4 major depressive episode symptoms, minimum symptom duration of 2 weeks or more; the core symptom may be either depressed mood or anhedonia
Requires a minimum of 2 years with numerous periods of depressive symptoms and numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms, none meeting criteria for major depressive or manic episode
Focused history questions; consider toxicology screening if intoxication is suspected

list.listitem: Dysthymia in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual-5 (DSM-5) now falls under the category of PDD. This disorder includes both dysthymia and chronic MDD This change was due to an inability to find scientifically meaningful differences between these two conditions. In fact, there is continued disagreement about whether dysthymia is a single disorder or represents a heterogeneous group of depressive, anxiety and/or personality conditions.

Core symptom: depressed mood for most of the day, indicated by subjective account or observation by others, for more days than not, for at least 2 years in adults or at least 1 year for children and adolescents. In children and adolescents, the mood can be irritable.

During this period, the patient must also have 2 or more of the following: poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy or fatigue, low self-esteem, poor concentration or difficulty making decisions, feelings of hopelessness.
During the 2-year period, the patient has never been without the symptoms for more than 2 months at a time.
Because dysthymia is now combined with chronic MDD, major depression may precede the disorder, and major depressive episodes may occur during PDD.
Patient has never had a manic, hypomanic, or mixed (manic/depressive) episode, and symptoms have never met criteria for cyclothymic disorder.
Mood disturbance does not occur exclusively during the course of a psychotic disorder.
Symptoms are not the physiologic result of a substance or a general medical condition.
Symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning.
Individuals whose symptoms meet major depressive disorder criteria for 2 years should also be given a diagnosis of PDD in addition to MDD.

At least 2 years of persistently depressed mood is the most prominent characteristic. Most patients also experience chronic fatigue, low energy, guilt or a sense of worthlessness, and difficulty concentrating or making decisions. Many patients also report sleep disturbance and poor libido.
Mild but chronic symptoms lead to significant distress or cumulative functional impairment.

Consider major depressive disorder (MDD) if suicidality, life-threatening behaviors, or severe functional impairment are present. Consider other DSM-5 diagnoses if history of mania or psychosis is present.

Authors of a review of PDD found several features that help distinguish chronic depressions from non-chronic MDD. Antecedent factors were earlier onset of depression, greater childhood maltreatment, and higher rates of chronic depression among family members. Concurrent factors included social isolation, greater functional impairment, and higher rates of psychiatric and somatic co-morbidity. These authors also noted that most rating and self-report inventories for depression have limited usefulness for identifying PDD.
Check the CBC and TSH levels to rule out anemia and hypothyroidism upon initial presentation and in cases of acute worsening of symptoms.
Check a toxicology screen if intoxication or drug use is suspected.
While there are no validated screening tools specifically for persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia), validated tools for depression include the PHQ, PHQ-2 and a tool specific for the elderly.
The General Behavior Inventory, as a self-report measure developed to screen for chronic mood disorders, may be useful because it assesses symptoms based on trait rather than a discrete episode.

Among adolescents, the lay-administered Composite International Diagnostic Interview Version 3.0 demonstrates good concordance with clinical diagnosis based on the Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children for major depressive episode/dysthymic disorder (area under the ROC curve 0.86, excellent classification accuracy).
See algorithm in .
Consider medication for all patients with persistent depressive disorder (see ). A
Select antidepressant medication after considering the following factors: clinical history, expected side effects,patient preference, cost, and availability (see Depression chapter) . C
Only about half of patients respond to the first medication used,so re-evaluate effectiveness at least monthly until symptom remission, and adjust therapy as indicated (see and ). A
Consider maintenance treatment for all patients with dysthymia (see ). C

Antidepressants are an effective treatment for dysthymia; consider medication therapy for all patients (see ). In a meta-analysis, there was a greater risk ratio for response to antidepressant therapy vs. placebo in patients with dysthymic disorder versus MDD.

Similar efficacy was reported by Cochrane authors for different groups of drugs including tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), monoamine oxidase inhibitors (eg, moclobemide) and other drugs (sulpiride, amineptine, and ritanserin) with a NNT of about 5.
Select an antidepressant after considering the following factors: clinical history, expected side effects, patient preference, and cost/availability (see Depression chapter).

Only half of patients respond to the first medication used,so re-evaluate effectiveness at least monthly until symptom remission occurs (see ). Adjust therapy as indicated by clinical situation, side effects, and safety from suicidal ideation (see and ).

More patients discontinued imipramine due to adverse effects compared with SSRIs and placebo in an RCT;however, systematic reviews have shown mixed results, with TCAs demonstrating both higher and similardiscontinuation rates compared with SSRIs. SSRIs, however, can cause akathisia and sexual dysfunction that may be severe and enduring.

The serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor duloxetine was effective vs. placebo for patients with chronic non-major depression with respect to short-term symptom improvement and remittance. There was no improvement in global functioning or social adjustment.

Antipsychotic medications such as amisulpride, a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist used in patients with schizophrenia, can also be considered for treatment of PDD. Based on 5 RCTs, there is evidence of benefit of low-dose amisulpride (second-generation antipsychotic) for people with dysthymia.

In a meta-analysis of 45 trials, fluoxetine (odds ratio [OR] 2.94), paroxetine (OR 3.79), sertraline (OR 4.47), moclobemide (OR 6.98), imipramine (OR 4.53), ritanserin (OR 2.35), amisulpride (OR 5.63), and acetyl-l-carnitine (OR 5.67) were significantly more effective than placebo for PDD. With respect to comparative trials, moclobemide (2.38) and amisulpride (1.92) performed better than fluoxetine, and sertraline (0.57) and amisulpride (0.53) showed a lower dropout rate than imipramine.

L-Acetylcarnitine (LAC) was as effective as fluoxetine in improving symptoms in one RCT of 80 patients with dysthymic disorder. LAC is synthesized from the amino acid carnitine and involved in fatty acid metabolism; it is found in many tissues including the brain.
Authors of a recent systematic review concluded that SSRIs and SNRIs are more effective than placebo for dysthymia treatment, and LAC should be investigated further for PDD in elderly patients.
In patients with comorbid alcohol use disorders, tricyclics and nefazodone (vs. placebo) appear effective in treating dysthymia but possibly not SSRIs.
St. John's wort is more effective than placebo, but there are insufficient data to compare it with other agents.
5-Hydroxytryptophan and tryptophan appear to be more effective than placebo, but higher quality studies are needed to evaluate efficacy and safety better.
Individual psychotherapy is used, but there is little supportive evidence.

In an RCT of 268 patients with early-onset chronic depression who were not taking antidepressant medication, highly structured specific psychotherapy (Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy) was more effective than nonspecific therapy with respect to depression scores (significant adjusted mean difference of −2.51) and remission (27 of 124 [21.8%] vs. 14 of 111 [12.6%]; adjusted odds ratio, 3.55; 95% CI 1.61-7.85).

Patients who are more severely depressed and have experienced moderate-severe childhood trauma may be more likely to benefit from Cognitive Behavioral System of Psychotherapy based on profiling of 237 patients with early-onset PDD who were not taking antidepressant medication and were enrolled in an RCT.

In the meta-analysis noted above, interpersonal psychotherapy combined with medication outperformed medication alone in chronic MDD but not in dysthymia. Interpersonal psychotherapy was less effective than medication (0.48) and cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) (0.45).
Group psychotherapy added to fluoxetine significantly improved interpersonal, cognitive, and global psychosocial functioning but not other dysthymia symptomatology in an unblinded RCT.
Group CBT did not significantly improve dysthymia symptoms when used either alone or in combination with sertraline.

In a meta-analysis of 4 studies, group CBT reduced depressive symptoms in older adults with sub-threshold depression during treatment, but did not reduce the risk of depressive disorder during follow-up.
Exercise has been shown to decrease depression symptoms, but it has not been studied exclusively in patients with dysthymia.

High- and low-intensity aerobic exertion is more effective than flexibility training; compared with flexibility exercises, NNT = 5 patients performing high-intensity aerobics to have a significant reduction in mean Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression score.

Improvements in mood following dietary intervention compared to a comparison group were found in a meta-analysis based on 5 studies; however, there was heterogeneity in both the dietary intervention and the outcomes measured.

PDD treatment is divided into 3 consecutive phases: acute (from initial presentation to complete remission), continuation (4-5 months of effective treatment dose or psychotherapeutic regimen after remission to prevent relapse), and maintenance (ongoing treatment beyond continuation phase to prevent recurrence; see ).
Consider maintenance treatment for all patients with dysthymia due to their chronic depression symptoms and significant cumulative functional impairment (see ).

Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine whether continued or maintained pharmacotherapy with antidepressants was a robust treatment for preventing relapse and recurrence in people with PDD due to moderate-high risk of study bias and clinical heterogeneity. Limited data suggested that psychotherapy might be effective compared to no treatment.

Consider psychiatric referral for treatment-resistant symptoms; concomitant psychiatric disorders (eg, eating disorders or substance abuse); and development of MDD, psychosis, or suicidality (see Depression chapter).
Nearly all people with persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) will also experience a major depressive episode during their lifetime. A
Approximately 20% are hospitalized, 20% attempt suicide, and 1% complete suicide in a 5-year period. B
Approximately 50% of treated patients recover within 3 to 5 years; roughly 40% of patients in remission will relapse within 2 years. B

All-cause mortality was higher for Singaporean individuals aged >60 years with subthreshold depression (9.9% of the population) at 10-year follow-up compared to those without major depression or subthreshold depression.
Almost all (94%) of patients with PDD will experience at least one lifetime major depressive episode.
In a study of 1,970 Chinese women with MDD, the 354 women with a history of dysthymia had more severe MDD than those without, more episodes of MDD, and greater co-morbidity for anxiety disorders.
Approximately 20% of patients with dysthymia will attempt suicide, and 1% will complete suicide during a 5-year period.

In a Singaporean population cohort study of 1070 persons aged ≥60 years, adjusted all-cause mortality hazard ratio was 1.73 (95% CI 1.11-2.67) for major depression (5.1% of the population) and 1.38 (95% CI 0.96-1.97) for subthreshold depression (9.9% of the population) compared to those without these diagnoses at 10-year follow-up.
Approximately 22% of patients with dysthymia will have a psychiatric hospitalization over a 5-year period.
Approximately 50% of dysthymic outpatients receiving psychiatric services will recover within 5 years.
However, approximately 40% to 45% of patients with remitted dysthymia will relapse within 2 years.
Episode length also appears to predict poorer response to pharmacotherapy.

Monitor for the following: development of suicidality , dysthymia symptom status, response to treatment, functional status (occupational, social, etc.), development of side effects, adherence to treatment, signs of switch to mania, other psychiatric or general medical conditions that may influence symptoms/treatment.
Determine monitoring frequency by considering severity of symptoms, patient treatment adherence, availability of social supports, and the presence of comorbid general medical problems (see ).
Acute phase : follow-up visit every 1 to 4 weeks, monitor patients closely for side effects, clinical condition, and safety from suicidal ideation (see ).
Continuation phase : follow-up visit every month, according to clinical condition and treatments being provided (see ).
Maintenance phase : follow-up visit every 2 to 3 months, according to clinical condition and treatments being provided (see and ).
Same diagnostic criteria for PDD as in younger patients.
A general recommendation is to start antidepressant medications with half the recommended initial adult dose.
Same diagnostic criteria during and after pregnancy and same treatment recommendations, except as noted below.
Among women with prior depression who stopped antidepressants during pregnancy, there was a 5-fold higher risk of relapse during pregnancy.
No association is found between in utero antidepressant exposure and subsequent child cognitive dysfunction.
Benefits of treatment should be weighed against risk; treatment is recommended according to the usual depression guidelines (see Major Depressive Disorder), with exceptions noted below.

SSRIs (except paroxetine; see below) are generally considered safe during pregnancy; the safety of fluoxetine is especially well studied. Fluoxetine does not lead to increased major malformations or spontaneous abortion; first-trimester exposure may lead to increased minor anomalies; third-trimester exposure may lead to increased premature delivery, short-term neonatal complications, low birth weight, and shorter birth length.Use of SSRIs in the third trimester has been reported to cause withdrawal symptoms in newborns (eg, jitteriness, increased muscle tone, irritability, altered sleep patterns, tremors and difficulty eating).
In a small case-control study, SSRIs taken after 20 weeks of gestation were associated with a 6-times higher risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.
Paroxetine is FDA class D due to increased risk of congenital malformations, particularly cardiac septal defects.
Bupropion use in pregnancy does not increase malformation risk but may increase risk of spontaneous abortion.
Venlafaxine does not increase major malformation risk.
Breastfeeding while on SSRIs results in some infant exposure via breast milk; sertraline, paroxetine, and most TCAs are considered safe.
Symptoms are similar in children, although diagnostic criteria differ, with a depressed or irritable mood duration requirement of at least 1 year instead of 2 years.
Increased risk of suicidal thinking and behavior is observed among children, adolescents, and young adults with dysthymia up to age 24 years.

A 2022 guideline on assessment and treatment of MDD and PDD from the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP) suggests offering cognitive-behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy to adolescents and children with MDD or PDD. They note that there is a paucity of studies on PDD, but recommend use of SSRIs (except paroxetine), preferably fluoxetine, for adolescents and children with MDD.

Authors of a meta-analysis of psychological interventions for children and adolescents with PPD found 12 trials with 1,576 subjects and concluded overall treatment benefit (NNT 8.4), but no difference in subsequent incidence of MDD. There was moderate to high study heterogeneity and significant risk of bias. However, there was no clear benefit in the two studies of children under age 12 years.

AACAP suggests that continued fluoxetine alone or cognitive-behavioral therapy plus continued fluoxetine could be offered to adolescents and children responding to acute treatment with fluoxetine to prevent relapse/recurrence of MDD.
